analysis.one_liner: Tightens federal oversight of for-profit colleges and lets defrauded student borrowers erase their loans.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in two House committees without a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended, despite 23 Democratic sponsors in a Democratic-controlled House.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have imposed new rules on for-profit colleges, the schools that receive most of their money from federal student aid and GI Bill benefits. It would have restored a rule limiting how much of a school's revenue can come from federal funds, reviewed for-profit schools that rebrand as nonprofits, required career programs to lead to real jobs, banned schools from forcing students into arbitration instead of court, created a federal complaint system for students, and let borrowers cancel loans if a school misled them [S2][S3]. It never received a hearing or vote in either committee it was sent to [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Students at for-profit colleges — a population that skews toward low-income, first-generation, and veteran students — plus taxpayers who currently absorb the cost when students default on loans from low-quality programs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students and veterans at for-profit colleges

how_it_helps.text: Restores the '85/15 rule' requiring for-profit schools to draw at least 15% of revenue from non-federal sources, and counts GI Bill and Defense Department benefits as federal money, closing what the bill calls the GI Bill loophole [S2][S3].

Lets borrowers apply to cancel federal loans when a school misled them or engaged in other misconduct, and allows state attorneys general to file group claims on behalf of many borrowers at once [S2][S3].
Bars schools receiving federal money from forcing students into mandatory arbitration and from limiting students' right to sue in court [S2][S3].

Creates an enforcement unit inside federal student aid operations, a centralized complaint tracking system with anonymous reporting, and an annual public 'warning list' of for-profit colleges with records of illegal or predatory conduct [S2][S3].

Requires career education programs to meet debt-to-earnings standards so students are prepared for 'gainful employment,' and requires a review process when a for-profit school converts to nonprofit status to prevent abuse of that label [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: For-profit college companies, their investors, lead-generation and online-program-management contractors, and — where schools collapse or claims succeed — federal taxpayers who absorb forgiven loan balances.

drawbacks.text: Expanding loan forgiveness shifts the cost of discharging loans onto federal taxpayers when a school's misconduct leaves borrowers with unpayable debt [S2][S3].

The revenue cap counting GI Bill and Defense Department funds as federal money could force some schools — including ones serving large veteran populations — out of federal aid entirely, which critics said could reduce education options for those students [S2][S3].
The debt-to-earnings and disclosure requirements impose significant compliance and reporting costs on institutions, costs that smaller schools argue are hardest for them to absorb [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For students and veterans at for-profit colleges, the protections — loan cancellation for misconduct, the right to sue, a complaint system, and public warning lists — address documented harms like high debt, low graduation and job-placement rates, and misleading recruiting. The real costs fall on the for-profit education industry and, in the case of loan forgiveness, partly on taxpayers. The main design question is whether cutting off federal money to low-performing schools improves outcomes for enrolled students or simply removes their current option; the bill includes warnings and appeals processes to soften that transition.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Education and Labor and Judiciary committees and then to a Judiciary subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced June 26, 2019 by Rep. Susie Lee with 8 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S1][S3].
It was referred to the Committee on Education and Labor and the Committee on the Judiciary on the day of introduction [S5].
On July 30, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, its last recorded action [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote was ever held, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit colleges and their contractors came out ahead: no new revenue limits, no gainful-employment tests, no mandatory access to court for students, and no expanded loan cancellation took effect. Students and veterans kept whatever existing protections were in place.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats in the Democratic-controlled chamber, but no vote was ever held, so the party split was never tested on the floor.

industries.note: The bill caps the federal share of their revenue (counting GI Bill and Defense funds), reviews conversions to nonprofit status, requires gainful-employment standards, and creates a public warning list. These rules target the sector's core model of collecting most revenue from federal student aid while students often carry debt without completing marketable credentials.

industries.industry: Lead generators and online program managers
industries.note: The bill defines these recruiting and outsourcing contractors for the first time and subjects them and revenue-sharing arrangements to oversight, threatening a business built on selling prospective-student names to schools.

Servicers would fall under a centralized complaint tracking system with mandatory responses and public reporting of complaint volumes, adding scrutiny and compliance costs, though they would not lose revenue outright.
